extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, writers, comedians and general readers researching satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for understanding, analysing, and producing satirical work across media (literature, theatre, cartoons, digital media), including topics, techniques, legal/ethical boundaries, and measures of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of satire depends on state tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: La reale esistenza della satira in una società deriva ... dal margine di tolleranza espresso dai poteri punitivi dello Stato. (The real existence of satire in a society derives from the margin of tolerance expressed by the State's punitive powers.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: the 1835 ban on political satire in France and governmental crackdowns; indicates that whether satire can be practiced publicly depends on legal/political tolerance and repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political function: influencing public opinion and government
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire rose the daunting question of what role public opinion would play in government ... satirists criticized government activities, exposed ambiguities, and forced administrators to clarify or establish policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion for satirical effectiveness: does the work engage public opinion, provoke debate, or prompt administrative/political responses? Example: satire as a voice in favor of public political debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary topical targets of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion, politics, and sexuality are the primary stuff of literary satire; other common targets include housing, food, fuel supplies, poverty, inflation, public services, and national stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing satire, consider whether topic choice aligns with tradition and whether the subject is socially salient or politically charged; scatological and bodily topics are also historically common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sfottò (mockery) and genuine satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Sfottò is a bonaria caricature that highlights superficial tics and traits without attacking ideology or fundamental behavior; genuine satire analyzes and grotesquely exposes behaviour, ideology, hypocrisy and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: work that only lampoons external quirks (sfottò) may amuse but fails as transformative critique; strong satire should target underlying positions and practices, not only surface mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of parody: shallow vs deep
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies can be 'shallow' as well as 'deep' — shallow parody attacks surface faults or may function as a faint praise, while deep parody criticizes fundamental aspects of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether parody engages only stylistic surface (possibly flattering) or advances substantive critique of the target's assumptions, values, or structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scatology and the grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirists have utilized scatological and bathroom humour and the grotesque body (e.g., projecting scatological degradation onto aristocracy) as political and popular representational devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize scatology/grotesque as legitimate historical techniques in satire; evaluate whether such devices serve critical aims or are gratuitous shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of biting (tone and harshness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire exhibits varying 'degrees of biting' — from mild Horatian humor to harsher Juvenalian attack — which shape its tone and audience reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tonal choices and intended audience: milder irony may persuade broad publics, biting invective may mobilize or alienate; the degree of bite is a deliberate rhetorical parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of satire by the reaction it provokes
rubrics_metrics.description: La satira vera si vede dalla reazione che suscita. (True satire is seen by the reaction it provokes.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness metric: strong satire often elicits strong reactions (controversy, censorship, policy discussion). Examples include bans, public scandals, or official complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as practice in the public sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Satiric expression takes place in the public sphere and speaks from a position of public opinion — drawing audiences into new practices of representative government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the satirical work participates in public debate, invites civic engagement, or functions merely as private entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal foundations and limits of satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Il diritto di satira trova il suo fondamento negli artt. 21 e 33 della Costituzione ... i suoi limiti di liveità sono ben più ampi di quelli propri del diritto di cronaca. (Right to satire grounded in constitutional freedoms; its expressive limits are broader than ordinary reporting.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing satire, consider jurisdictional constitutional protections, defamation/copyright/impersonation laws and real-world cases (e.g., lawsuits against satirists, corporate defamation claims). Legal protection is broader than news reporting but not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation and 'mock news' techniques carry risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical impersonation of bodies (e.g., mimicking official publications or news formats such as The Onion) is a common technique but has legal and credibility implications (impersonation bills/examples cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity of satirical signals (disclaimers, genre cues) and legal exposure: ambiguous mimicry may cause real-world confusion or legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium shapes satirical form and possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire appears in literature, theatre, political cartoons, television, film, videogames and online sites — each medium offers different satirical affordances (e.g., GTA's running satirical commentary; mock news websites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose medium aware of its conventions; evaluate how medium-specific devices (visual caricature, gameplay, serialized sketches) affect satirical aims and audience reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's ambivalent relationship to power
rubrics_metrics.description: Power both enjoys (finds pleasure in being mocked) and fears satire: political contexts can make satire a resource or prompt repression; power may co-opt, enjoy or clamp down on satirical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether satire reinforces or challenges power; be mindful of co-option (satire making targets 'sympathetic') versus subversive critique that endangers power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire's persuasive/argumentative voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire's persuasive voice can do rhetorical work beyond entertainment, mobilizing opinions and framing political critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate argumentative structure: does the satirical piece construct claims, reveal contradictions, or simply entertain? Effective satire combines humor with substantive rhetorical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritualized and cultural contexts for sanctioned mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Many societies allow ritualized mockery (Saturnalia, Feast of Fools, Carnival) — sanctioned temporal spaces where mocking institutions is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production/evaluation should account for cultural forms that legitimize satire; timing, festival context, and ritual conventions affect acceptability and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques and devices: parody, caricature, irony, exaggeration, grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Common satirical devices include parody, caricature, irony, exaggeration and grotesque depiction — used to expose hypocrisy and absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how devices are employed: do they illuminate a target's vice/contradiction or merely produce cheap laughs? Examples: caricature of politicians, parodic news headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and historical sensitivity of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire can address extreme or sensitive subjects (e.g., Holocaust humour); such usage raises ethical questions about offensiveness and historical context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether satire of traumatic or marginalized subjects is justified by critical aim and handled with contextual awareness; poor handling may be destructive rather than illuminating.
